doc.title: Chico Freeman interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: What Muhal Richard Abrams taught him: jazz history
summary: Despite his modern reputation, Muhal had him transcribe Willie the Lion Smith, James P. Johnson and Armstrong, teaching that one must know the rules to break them.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Was the association with Muhal Richard Abrams — he was pretty modern, I mean pretty progressive, that whole contingent of players is that right?
And did you like that kind of freedom in your music?

Yes I did. I mean it was a new thing for me. I mean I had been playing a lot of straight ahead and pretty mainstream I guess, along with a lot of the R&B stuff and things like that. When I met him he showed me new ways of doing things which was quite startling. Actually it sort of got to me because his way of teaching was — as modern as he was, as he is — his way of teaching was always to go back in history. From him I learned more about the history of jazz than anything else. He took me back to Willie “The Lion” Smith and James P. Johnson and Louis Armstrong. I used to have to transcribe their solos. I mean the things I had to do with him, you would think, a lot of people would think, because of Muhal’s reputation in his music, that he being so modern, that this was not likely, but he is very versed on the history of the music in all aspects. Historically speaking as well as musically speaking. And so that’s what I was studying with him and doing that. And in showing me these things, because he always said if you don’t study the

history you’re bound to repeat it, and if you want to do things different you’ve got to first know the rules to break them, and all of that. So that was his premise that he operated from. And so it was a great experience for me.
